The player can change the volume of each note by touch, and can alter the resonance with a hand stop, a knee lever or a pedal. Its timbre is softer than the modern piano's and its sustaining shorter, so a sudden loud note stands out the more, because its colour and its volume both differ and it decays quickly. The range has grown from about four octaves when the instrument was invented to about five in Mozart's day and about six and a half in Beethoven's late years; the timbre is uneven across the range, the bass slightly buzzing, the treble slightly tinkling and the middle rounder, whereas the modern piano is more even.

Because the construction was complex and costly, it was at first found at the Portuguese and Spanish courts, and in 1732 Lodovico Giustini published sonatas written specifically for the piano. From the end of the eighteenth century it went on developing into the modern piano, and after the twentieth century it was revived by period-instrument performance.

The fortepiano is the forerunner of the piano, a chordophone, and comes from Italy. It sounds when leather-covered hammers strike light strings; its case is lighter than a modern piano's and early instruments mostly have no metal frame. Pressing a key drives the hammer against the string and lifts the damper, and releasing the key stops the sound, and the volume can be changed by touch. The control is not necessarily a pedal; hand stops and knee levers were also used. From the late eighteenth to the early nineteenth century Classical composers such as Haydn and Mozart wrote piano music for it, and it was also used at court and for royal performance; today it is mostly found in period-instrument performance.
